snip.t: Multiple Sclerosis (MS): MS is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the protective covering of nerve fibers in the central nervous system.

Potential causes include genetic/chromosomal conditions, congenital brain abnormalities, prenatal exposures or infections, prematurity or perinatal complications, severe early malnutrition, central nervous system infections, traumatic brain injury and some metabolic disorders.

Absolute contraindications to fibrinolytics include previous hemorrhagic stroke, ischemic stroke within six months, known central nervous system neoplasm or vascular malformation, recent major trauma/surgery, active internal bleeding, or suspected aortic dissection.

snip.t: Localization symptoms: Cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea (respiratory); dysuria, flank pain (urinary); photophobia, neck stiffness, confusion (central nervous system); abdominal pain, diarrhea (gastrointestinal); joint pains or rashes (rheumatologic/arboviral).
These indicate central nervous system (CNS) infections like cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, or tuberculoma.
Central nervous system: Meninges, blood‑brain barrier — Limited drug penetration, CSF turnover
Central nervous system: Hyperexcitability (storm) vs cerebral edema, reduced mental status (coma)

qs.q: Most excitatory neurotransmission in the central nervous system is mediated by
qs.e: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS. GABA and glycine are the major inhibitory amino-acid neurotransmitters.

qs.q: How does tetanus toxin reach inhibitory interneurons in the central nervous system?
qs.e: Tetanus toxin enters peripheral motor nerve terminals and undergoes retrograde axonal transport to the central nervous system, where it blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters.

qs.q: Regarding viral infection of the central nervous system (CNS), one of the statements below is false
o: Meningitis may occur together with encephalitis
Enteroviruses are one of the commonest causes of CNS infections in childhood
Herpes simplex encephalitis is a post-infectious encephalomyelitis
Measles encephalitis is a post-infectious encephalomyelitis
qs.e: HSV encephalitis is a DIRECT viral encephalitis — the virus actively replicates within brain parenchyma. It is NOT post-infectious. Measles encephalitis (ADEM) IS a post-infectious autoimmune encephalomyelitis.

qs.q: A 60-year-old with established CLL complains of headaches and blurred vision. Which diagnostic procedure is indicated to assess for central nervous system involvement?
o: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid cytology
qs.e: CSF cytology directly detects leukaemic cell infiltration of the central nervous system.
